stories.title: Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing scheduled to visit Cambodia from Sept 11 to 12: Sources
stories.summary: Myanmar’s leader Min Aung Hlaing will visit Cambodia from Sept 11-12, continuing diplomatic trips to ASEAN countries to gain regional legitimacy after the 2021 coup. His visits face criticism from activists and rights groups who say hosting him legitimises his military regime despite ongoing violence in Myanmar. ASEAN wants Myanmar to implement the Five-Point Consensus, but Min Aung Hlaing has rejected that plan, using bilateral visits to bypass ASEAN summit bans and strengthen ties selectively. Myanmar junta chief-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing is scheduled to visit Cambodia from Sept 11 to 12, after a trip to Vietnam from Sept 4 to 6. High-level sources in Phnom Penh confirmed the Cambodia dates with The Straits Times on Sept 3. While Phnom Penh was earlier reported to have extended an invitation to Myanmar, the dates for the visit haven’t been confirmed until now. With these trips, Min Aung Hlaing will have visited four ASEAN states in three months. And Cambodia will be the eighth country he will visit since assuming the presidency earlier in 2026, as he seeks greater legitimacy and regional re-engagement. These international trips come even as members of the Myanmar diaspora and activists stage protests outside Thai embassies in cities like London, Seoul and Tokyo to urge Bangkok not to legitimise the Myanmar regime. In mid-August, Phnom Penh had said Min Aung Hlaing would be visiting Cambodia in order “to strengthen the friendship between Cambodia and Myanmar”. “Cooperation between the two countries is necessary and mutually beneficial,” Chea Thyrith, spokesperson for the Senate president, was quoted as saying in the Cambodian media. Min Aung Hlaing, 70, has launched a diplomatic push to solidify his position following the junta’s 2021 coup.

stories.title: Outcry over ‘weapons of love’ forces Hong Kong charity to scrap student contest
stories.summary: A leading Hong Kong charity has called off a student eco-bag design contest meant to counter domestic violence following public backlash over its directive for pupils to draw inspiration from objects commonly linked to household abuse. Po Leung Kuk confirmed on Thursday that it had scrapped the competition, which was organised by its family crisis support service and funded by the Social Welfare Department.
